# Caring more is the only moat left

We had to tear the answer pages out of my son's maths book.

He had been doing all of his homework from the back of the book. Every exercise was correct, of course. And he had not thought about a single problem.

It was always easier to go to the answers than to think about the problem.

It's also what most of us now do with AI. We open the tool, type something like "build me an app", and thirty seconds later there is an app. We go straight to the answer and accept what comes back. It's easy. But is it done well?

## Everyone looked sideways

None of this started with AI.

Between 2012 and 2018, six luxury brands changed their logos. Each of the old ones carried decades of history, and you could recognise every one of them without reading the name. Six years later, the six had ended up with logos that looked almost the same.

There's a word for it: blanding, from bland, as in flavourless. It describes brands that all end up looking the same while trying to look modern. And nobody decided to be the same. None of those brands wanted to look like the others. Each one looked sideways, saw what was working for the others, and did the same.

I lived my own version of it. Every designer went to the same place for inspiration: Dribbble.[^1] We copied the best work. There was even a name for one kind of copying, the rebound: you recreated someone else's design and tried to make it better, and there were contests to redesign other people's work, only better. After a while, all the apps started to look alike. We called it the Dribbble effect.

Each wave has been faster and wider than the last. The luxury brands took six years. Dribbble was one website and one profession. With AI, anyone can build something in five minutes, and because everyone goes to the same source, everyone gets the same product.

![Three waves of sameness: luxury brands over six years, Dribbble across one profession, AI for everyone in five minutes](images/t1-ss-1.png)
*Each wave of sameness was faster and wider than the one before.*

## The average, handed to everyone

These tools learned from everything that was ever published. They know what has worked for everyone else, and they know nothing about us. When we ask for something and give nothing else, they hand back what is most common: the average. And everyone who asks gets the same one.

I gave the same brief to ChatGPT, Claude and Figma Make, once for a music app and once for a bank app, and I got the same app back each time.[^2] None of the three tools knew a thing about the brand, who the users were, or what code already existed.

Now think of real products in those categories. Spotify, Apple Music and SoundCloud are all music apps. Revolut, Monzo and Nubank are all bank apps. Same category, completely different products, each with its own identity and its own customers. That difference is what the tools can't give us when we bring nothing to them.

Products copy each other too. Show someone AFFiNE with the name hidden and there's a good chance they'll tell you it's Notion. AFFiNE, AppFlowy and Anytype are real products from different companies, and next to Notion they share the same grey sidebar, the same page title, the same blocks and the same checkboxes.[^3] They copied the one everyone already knew.

That is AI blanding, and this time it reaches everyone.

## What caring more looks like

A friend of mine is an osteopath. He knew nothing about programming, and he had a problem no product solved, not even something that would connect to the device he uses with his patients. So he built something small with AI and showed it to me. I told him to keep going, and I gave him a few tips.

He never wrote a line of code. What he had was years of living that problem every day. His product now handles patients, appointments and prescriptions, connects to his device, works on desktop and mobile, and already has two clients.

This is uncomfortable for those of us who build products for other people, and I include myself: today, someone who really knows a business can build a good product more easily than someone who only builds what they're asked to. That knowledge isn't on the internet. It's in people. The way out is to go and get it before we open the tool: talk to the people who use it, understand the business, ask questions.

The second story is from our work. On one project, creating a new component took weeks: requirements, exploring solutions, testing, development and QA, with the information scattered everywhere. So we built a design system accelerator that puts all of that context in one place the machine can read. The same process went from weeks to hours, with the same scope both times: one component, from ticket to reviewed pull request, QA included.

It is fast because the machine has the context. And it is done well because there is always a name next to the decision. It reads the ticket, asks questions and proposes three options, and you pick one. It writes the code and runs the checks, and you review what it flags. Nothing is merged until an engineer approves. It's the opposite of asking a tool that knows nothing about us for an app.

> [PULL QUOTE] If it isn't written where the machine can read it, it doesn't exist.

The third story is the one that worries me most in a company like ours.

We ran a short design sprint with people from one of our clients, in different roles and none of them designers. None of them had ever opened a design tool. They had one real problem from their own business, the design thinking framework, the same AI tools they already used, and one facilitator per group from our designers and product people, there as a guide rather than a creator.

Every group built a working prototype, and no two were alike: each group came back with a different solution, based on a different user context. Same problem, same afternoon. With one team only, we would have stopped at the first idea.

Then we swapped the teams, and that's where the prototypes got good. Each team tested another team's prototype. AI recorded the session and organised the improvements. People chose what went in, and at the end they presented the result themselves. AI was in every step, but in every round there was a person saying what was right and what wasn't.

People from a client, none of them designers, built working prototypes in one afternoon. If our job is only to do what we're asked, they no longer need us for it. What we brought that day was the method, the facilitation and the technical knowledge. The tools were the ones they already had.

The next story is about how finished a first result can look. We were hiring, and every candidate sent us a personal website: the same layout, the same gradient, the same sentences. I didn't know whether I was evaluating the person or Claude. They did nothing wrong. They all just did the same thing.

The last one is mine. We were making a marketing video for one of our accelerators, and most videos made with AI look alike now. Ours couldn't. I didn't want the first characters the tool offered me, so I ran a casting. I asked Higgsfield[^4] to create candidates, seventy-one of them, until I had the cast I wanted. One scene, on a boat, went through twenty-two versions. I kept two.

![Seventy-one casting candidates and twenty-two versions of one boat scene, of which two were kept](images/t1-ss-2.png)
*The casting and the boat scene from a marketing video for one of our accelerators.*

I could not deliver the first ones. AI did not save me work here. It let me try many more times, until it was the way I wanted.

Look at four of those stories together. Without AI, my friend wouldn't have his product, the component would still take weeks, people who had never opened a design tool wouldn't have working prototypes after one afternoon, and I wouldn't have made twenty-two versions of a boat. Those four are what I mean by caring more.

> [PULL QUOTE] AI gives the first version. The good version is our decision.

## A framework to keep

Human judgment still matters. I see four places where we are losing it, and they follow the order of the work. Four words, one acronym: KEEP. Because this is how we keep what is ours.

Before you open the tool, **know** the problem better than the tool does. When you set it up, **encode** your context into the machine: what already exists, the brand, the design system, the code and the decisions already made. While you work, **explore** beyond what you were asked: if AI makes one version cheap, it also makes ten versions cheap, so the job becomes looking further and choosing well. Before you deliver, **polish** until the quality is there, because the first result already looks finished. Not everywhere: where people feel it.

Lately, some of my best thinking happens in the car. I treat the drive like a call with a colleague. I switch to voice and just talk. I think out loud, it pushes back, I ask it to draft something. Twenty minutes of dead time turn into twenty minutes of real work. It doesn't feel like using an app. It feels like having someone in the passenger seat. And it isn't only the car. Even at my desk, I dictate whenever I can. We type around forty words a minute. We speak around one hundred and thirty.

My main tool isn't in the car yet. And that is the point: the products we build don't have to live only on a screen. We have to start imagining other experiences: other moments, other places, other ways to use what we build.

![When everyone has the same tools, the only thing others can't copy is people who care more](images/t1-ss-3.png)
*The tools are the same for everyone; the care is what others can't copy.*

If you lead a team, or if you build products: if all the time AI saves goes into delivering more of the same, we just get more things that look the same. Someone has to decide that part of that time goes back into the product, and protect it in the plan.

## Burberry went back

Remember the six logos from 2012 to 2018? Burberry was one of them. In 2023, it understood that looking like the others wasn't helping, and it went back to being itself.

The logo wasn't the fix. It was a signal of going back to what made it different. It took five years. We can choose now.

Keep caring.
